column3: Worldly preferences are real but the greater degrees belong to the Hereafter, preventing present rank from becoming an ultimate measure.
It grounds differentiated degrees in what people have done, offering a moral counterpart to the focus verse's differentiated worldly livelihood.
Jacob's deferred prayer for forgiveness does not clarify the distribution of livelihood, rank, or mercy.
God raises some above others in degrees as a test in what He has given, directly framing unequal provision as entrusted trial rather than self-made worth.
The immediate continuation imagines extravagant silver houses for disbelievers, showing that material abundance is not a sign of spiritual preference.
God's subjection of ships and rivers supplies human use, but it does not explain the social differentiation or mercy contrast in the focus verse.
Worldly splendor is a test, while the Lord's provision is better and more lasting; this directly resists treating visible wealth as true favor.
The immediate continuation adds doors and reclining couches to the hypothetical luxury of disbelievers, extending the focus verse's critique of material status.
The apportioned gates of Hell concern punishment classification, not worldly livelihood or social service.
God's differing elevation of messengers confirms that rank is divinely assigned, though it concerns prophetic distinction rather than worldly livelihoods.
God raises whom He wills in degrees, but the narrative's concern is knowledge and providence rather than the social purpose of unequal livelihood.
The oath by retreating celestial bodies does not illuminate distribution, rank, mercy, or accumulation.
The gathering of mingled peoples at the trumpet does not clarify differentiated provision in worldly life.
The immediate conclusion calls all such ornament merely the enjoyment of worldly life and reserves the Hereafter for the God-conscious.
The divine names the Most Merciful and Merciful support mercy as God's attribute, but do not address its relation to wealth or rank here.
The mention of the Lord's mercy to Zachariah identifies mercy as divine gift, without explaining social differentiation.
Its record of repeatedly sent prophets is part of the same surah's rejection pattern, but does not itself clarify livelihood or degrees.
The Merciful Lord's absolute authority over speech reinforces that mercy is not apportioned by human claimants.
God's grace and mercy are explicitly declared better than what people accumulate, directly echoing and explaining the focus verse's final valuation.
God raises believers and those given knowledge in degrees, showing elevated standing as His responsive bestowal rather than material privilege.
Mockery of the message does not clarify the focus verse's functional social service or distribution of livelihood.
Divine forgiveness and mercy are better than what people gather, closely paralleling the focus verse's contrast between mercy and accumulation.
The denial of a child for the Most Merciful supports the surah's theology of the Rahman, but adds little on livelihood or rank.
Degrees, forgiveness, and mercy present divine reward as more than a social ranking, though the verse does not concern worldly provision.
The succession and rejection of messengers do not explain unequal worldly livelihoods or their purpose.
Believers receive degrees, forgiveness, and generous provision from their Lord, contrasting God-given spiritual reward with inherited material status.
The universal questioning of deniers concerns accountability, not the distribution of mercy or livelihood.
The raised mountain and commands at the gate do not materially clarify the focus verse's hierarchy or accumulation contrast.
Within the surah, Paradise is inherited because of deeds, supplying an alternative to evaluating people by their worldly shares.
The praise and greeting of Paradise do not address differentiated livelihood or mercy versus accumulation.
Its promise of protection and fulfilled desire in both lives offers a broad contrast to transient worldly provision, but is not specific to social rank.
Prayer and spending from provision do not explain why livelihoods and degrees are distributed differently.
The division of affairs illustrates ordered divine apportionment, but not the human livelihoods or mutual service specified in the focus verse.
Idolatrous social bonds that turn to mutual rejection do not clarify functional hierarchy or the value of mercy over wealth.
The claim to be guided by ancestral custom states the resistance that the focus verse answers by denying elites authority to assign divine mercy.
God's lordship over Sirius does not explain worldly livelihood, degrees, or accumulation.
The raising of the Prophet's mention is a God-given elevation, but it is not a model of differentiated material livelihood.
Rain sent in measured amount shows provision under divine measure, though it does not address social rank or mutual service.
The promised gathering for judgment does not clarify how worldly livelihood or degrees are distributed.
The mutual alliance of wrongdoers shows a consequence of their earnings, but not the constructive interdependence described in the focus verse.
Pharaoh's household taking Moses concerns a providential narrative reversal, not distribution of mercy or livelihood.
The inability of false gods to avert harm does not clarify the focus verse's distribution or hierarchy.
Its use of the same service/mockery term highlights that ridicule is a distinct sense and should not be read into the focus verse's mutual service.
The appeal to earlier messengers denies worship of gods besides the Most Merciful, supporting the focus verse's premise that mercy belongs to God alone.
The speaker's forgiveness and honor from his Lord show divine bestowal of dignity, but do not address material differentiation.
Wealth and children are temporary adornment, whereas enduring good deeds are better with the Lord, directly challenging material accumulation as the measure of value.
Moses's fear and reassurance at the sign do not clarify the focus verse's distribution or degrees.
The oath by the city does not contribute to the distribution of livelihood, mercy, or rank.
Layered darkness is a metaphor for unbelief, not a clarification of social hierarchy or accumulated wealth.
The nearby call to remember God's favor in subjected transport makes human capacity a received gift, but only indirectly relates to livelihood shares.
The command to seek God's forgiveness confirms mercy as divine, without addressing its superiority to accumulated wealth or social rank.
The false promises among wrongdoers do not clarify God's distribution of livelihood or mercy.
The Most Merciful's knowledge of seen and unseen affirms the divine source of mercy, but not the focus verse's allocation argument.
Steadfast confession of God as Lord concerns faithful conduct rather than differentiated worldly shares.
The covenant and raised mountain do not clarify livelihood distribution or the purpose of social degrees.
The immediate preceding confession that the Creator will guide frames divine guidance and revelation as His gift, not something determined by social prestige.
The Lord's complete awareness of people supports accountability for their response to provision, but not the distribution itself.
God's judgment between disputants does not explain unequal livelihood or mutual service.
The certainty of the promised event does not clarify mercy, material accumulation, or social rank.
The youths ask their Lord for mercy and right guidance, identifying mercy as a divine gift but not relating it to worldly wealth.
Mocking believers is a negative counterpart to proper social relations, yet it does not illuminate the functional service in the focus verse.
Moses's mission to Pharaoh continues the surah's prophetic warning, but offers no direct explanation of provision or degrees.
The repeated challenge about the Lord's favors does not specifically clarify differentiated livelihood or mercy's priority over wealth.
Each person has degrees according to deeds and the Lord overlooks none of them, directly distinguishing accountable rank from arbitrary worldly prestige.
The Prophet's complaint to his Lord records the surah's rejection context, but not the focus verse's distribution of livelihood.
The stepwise drawing on of deniers is an adverse progression, only distantly related to the focus verse's degrees.
The covenant breach and devotion to the calf do not clarify livelihood allocation or mutual service.
A pleasing life is an outcome of final weighing, but it does not explain worldly means of living or social hierarchy.
The greater degree belongs to faith, migration, striving, and sacrifice, offering a moral measure distinct from material advantage.
Cities ruined after becoming insolent in their prosperity show that comfortable livelihood is neither permanent nor proof of divine approval.
The nearby command to acknowledge God's favor in subjected transport treats usable resources as received, but does not directly address unequal shares.
Naming the Most Merciful as the source of the following gifts supports the focus verse's claim that mercy is God's gift, not human property.
The parable of worldly life reaches its height of adornment before sudden loss, directly undercutting confidence in accumulated material splendor.
The bedding and coverings of Hell concern punishment imagery, not livelihood, service, or mercy.
The command to magnify the Lord does not clarify differentiated provision or social degrees.
The prohibition of suspicion, spying, and backbiting regulates social ethics but does not explain the focus verse's economic differentiation.
The appeal to Moses's Lord continues the surah's Pharaoh narrative, but has no direct bearing on shares of livelihood or mercy.
Divine blessings, mercy, and guidance for the patient identify mercy as a gift, without engaging accumulation or rank.
The water share apportioned between people gives a concrete instance of ordered distribution that prevents competing claims, though in a different setting.
Making the day for livelihood identifies livelihood as divinely ordered, but does not explain its unequal allocation.
The highest degrees are for believers who do righteous deeds, presenting a superior evaluative order to worldly status.
The command to judge by revelation and warning against partial departure do not clarify livelihood distribution or mutual service.
The Prophet's offer of better guidance and the audience's rejection continue the immediate argument against inherited elite criteria for receiving revelation.
The pairing of might and mercy identifies divine mercy with sovereign power, but does not address its contrast with amassed wealth.
God's nearness in mercy to those who do good identifies mercy as divine response, without explaining social degrees or provision.
The nearby declaration of God's dominion and return to Him supplies the surah's ultimate frame, but only indirectly relates to unequal livelihood.
The Lord's admonition, healing, guidance, and mercy name nonmaterial gifts whose value exceeds merely accumulated possessions.
The gathering and separation of idolaters from their partners concerns false worship, not livelihood or social rank.
The affluent of earlier towns defend inherited custom when warned; this is the immediate social pattern to which the focus verse denies control over divine mercy.
God's ability to gather dispersed creatures does not clarify the allocation of livelihood or mercy.
The teaching of magic and separation of spouses do not illuminate functional social differentiation or accumulated wealth.
The questioning of messengers on the Last Day concerns hidden knowledge, not provision or hierarchical worldly roles.
The Hereafter is declared better and more lasting, directly supporting the focus verse's refusal to treat worldly accumulation as the highest good.
The Lord's sight of a person supports divine knowledge of their course, but does not address unequal shares or mercy over wealth.
The poets' wandering in every valley does not clarify the focus verse's distribution, hierarchy, or mercy.
Faith in the signs of the Lord affirms receptivity to divine guidance, but does not explain material differentiation.
Pilgrimage procedures and compensations do not clarify how livelihoods, ranks, or mercy are apportioned.
The repeated question about the Lord's favors does not specifically explain the focus verse's distinction between mercy and accumulation.
The promised pure son is a gift from the Lord, showing divine bestowal but not worldly livelihood or hierarchy.
The proof and clear light sent from the Lord support revelation as a divine gift, directly relevant to the challenge over who may receive the Lord's mercy.
The elite objection that the Quran should have been sent to a great man from one of the two cities is the immediate question answered by 43:32.
The rejection of the truth as magic supplies the immediate setting for the elite demand that revelation be assigned by worldly prestige.
Pharaoh's claim to be better than Moses because of visible status and weak speech is a direct example of judging divine mission by worldly hierarchy.
Pharaoh demands golden bracelets and accompanying angels as signs of Moses's worth, closely paralleling the assumption that divine favor should track material display.
It forbids coveting the advantages God has given some over others and directs people to seek His bounty, directly addressing divinely differentiated shares.
God has favored some over others in provision, while the favored resist sharing it with those under their authority; it directly confronts the meaning of unequal provision.
The Lord expands and restricts provision for whom He wills with full awareness, directly grounding livelihood distribution in divine knowledge rather than human entitlement.
God expands and restricts provision, while people delight in worldly life despite its smallness beside the Hereafter; this closely supports both halves of 43:32.
God expands and restricts provision for whom He wills and knows all things, directly restating the divine control of livelihoods.
It explicitly asks whether people see that God expands and restricts provision for whom He wills, making unequal livelihood a sign rather than proof of merit.
The claim that greater wealth and children guarantee immunity is the precise false inference that 43:32 undermines.
The response that the Lord expands and restricts provision for whom He wills directly explains why wealth cannot establish spiritual privilege.
It states that wealth and children do not bring people near to God, providing a direct criterion against material rank.
God's expansion and restriction of provision, and His replacement of what is spent, further frame wealth as a managed divine gift.
It asks whether people know that God expands and restricts provision for whom He wills, directly matching the focus verse's distribution of livelihood.
God expands and restricts provision for whom He wills because He knows all things, supplying the theological basis for differentiated shares.
Each person is to spend according to what God has given, treating differing means as a practical responsibility rather than a rank claim.
The human assumption that abundance means divine honor is stated and then rejected, directly correcting a central misreading of livelihood.
The matching assumption that restricted provision means humiliation is likewise rejected, completing the correction of status judgments based on wealth.
Worldly life is made attractive to disbelievers who mock believers, while God provides without measure; it separates visible wealth from final standing.
The catalog of desired worldly goods identifies the appeal of wealth and children, but does not itself explain their distribution or value.
God gives and removes dominion and raises or lowers whom He wills, providing a broad sovereignty frame for worldly hierarchy.
God provides for whom He wills without account, supporting divine freedom in bestowing provision though outside the focus verse's social setting.
Wealth and children are explicitly a test, directly resisting their use as evidence of superior standing.
Wealth and children are not to impress believers because they can become a means of trial and punishment rather than favor.
The repeated warning not to admire wealth and children reinforces that visible abundance is not a reliable sign of divine approval.
Those given luxury pursued it and became wrongdoers, linking privileged ease with moral failure rather than spiritual preference.
The command concerning a town's affluent before its destruction warns that privileged groups can turn provision into corruption.
The contrast between two garden owners begins a sustained parable of unequal property whose true value is judged by God, not possession.
The wealthy garden owner treats his abundance as secure and enduring, exemplifying the false confidence in amassed goods rejected by 43:32.
The destruction of the garden shows accumulated property to be vulnerable and unable to secure its owner.
It concludes that protection and reward are with God, not wealth, directly reordering the value implied by the garden parable.
The disbeliever's boast of future wealth and children displays the same attempt to infer lasting favor from material status.
The Messenger is sent as mercy to the worlds, clarifying that the Lord's mercy at issue in the elite objection is divine revelation, not material rank.
The Quran is described as healing and mercy for believers, directly identifying revealed guidance as a form of the Lord's mercy.
The question whether wealth and children mean that God hastens good things for their possessors directly challenges status-based readings of abundance.
Its answer that they do not perceive completes the correction: material increase need not mean divine preference.
On the Day when wealth and children do not benefit, accumulated status is decisively subordinated to a sound heart before God.
The Messenger's mission to all people as bearer of good news and warning supports universal divine address, but only indirectly counters elite claims to privileged revelation.
Worldly life is described as adornment and competition in wealth and children before fading away, directly relativizing what people accumulate.
It forbids exultation over what one has been given and prideful boasting, supplying the ethical response to differentiated shares.
Wealth and children must not distract from God's remembrance, directly limiting the authority of accumulation over spiritual life.
Wealth and children are a trial, giving the focus verse's material shares an explicit test-oriented interpretation.
The grant of abundant wealth and present sons to a denier shows that extensive provision can coexist with rejection.
The denier's demand for still more after abundant gifts exposes accumulation as an insatiable and unreliable measure of favor.
The human being transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient, identifying the moral danger latent in wealth-based independence.
Rivalry in accumulating more distracts people until death, directly opposing the focus verse's preference for the Lord's mercy over what they gather.
The one who gathers and counts wealth wrongly imagines it will make him immortal, a concentrated critique of accumulation as security.
God singles out whom He wills for His mercy despite others' resentment of revelation sent down to believers, directly answering human claims over divine mercy.
All bounty is in God's hand and He gives it to whom He wills, directly denying that a social group can control the recipients of divine favor.
God selects for His mercy whom He wills and possesses immense bounty, closely paralleling the focus verse's challenge to human apportionment of mercy.
God knows best where to place His message, directly answering the claim that revelation should be assigned according to worldly rank.
The revealed Book is guidance and mercy for believers, identifying divine guidance as mercy rather than an honor allocated by social elites.
The parable contrasts a powerless dependent with one freely given good provision who spends from it, making provision a divine grant rather than self-originated status.
The Prophet is told not to turn toward the adornment of worldly life, directly limiting the pull of affluent status beside faithful devotion.
The Lord's recompense is better and He is the best of providers, offering a close value contrast between divine provision and human gain.
Whatever worldly thing people receive is temporary enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting.
Qarun's wealth makes him exultant and oppressive, showing that extraordinary material provision can become a moral danger rather than a mark of approval.
Qarun is commanded to seek the Hereafter through what God has given him and not to forget his worldly share, directly ordering wealth beneath final good.
Those who desire worldly life mistake Qarun's enormous fortune for good fortune, displaying the status judgment corrected by 43:32.
Those given knowledge answer that God's reward is better, explicitly replacing envy of wealth with the higher divine measure.
Observers learn that God expands and restricts provision for whom He wills, directly restating the focus verse's theology of distributed livelihood.
The parable asks whether people accept equal partners in their own provision, using human reluctance over shares to expose false claims about divine authority.
The question whether the Reminder was sent down upon him among them is a close parallel to the elite objection in 43:31-32 over the recipient of revelation.
The person who calls wealth a product of his knowledge is corrected: it is a test, directly opposing self-made readings of material abundance.
The Quran is guidance and healing for believers, further identifying the revealed message as divine mercy rather than a prize of worldly hierarchy.
The Quran is described as clear insight, guidance, and mercy for people of certainty, confirming the nonmaterial nature of the Lord's gift.
The objection that the Reminder was sent to one man among the people repeats the social resentment behind the demand to control who receives revelation.
Paradise and forgiveness are God's bounty given to whom He wills, supporting the principle that ultimate favor is not allocated by human status.
Faith brings a share of God's mercy and a guiding light, treating mercy and guidance as divine gifts rather than material accumulation.
God gives His bounty to whom He wills, supplying a concise general statement against human ownership of divine favor.
Preferring the worldly life is named as the error immediately corrected by the superiority and permanence of the Hereafter.
